title: Web Performance Small Examples
description: Use these small Web Performance examples with the tools described in each lesson. Read the expected result before you try a change.

examples.title: Measure before changing code
examples.description: A performance measurement is a clue about a real task.
examples.code:
Choose one page and one task.
Record the device and network setting.
Load it several times.
Write down what feels slow.
Change one cause and repeat the same test.
examples.output: A fair comparison can show whether a change helped that task instead of only changing a number by chance.

examples.title: Know the three web vital ideas
examples.description: Core Web Vitals describe loading, response to input and visual stability.
examples.code:
LCP: When the largest main content becomes visible.
INP: How quickly the page shows a response to interactions.
CLS: How much visible content unexpectedly moves.
examples.output: The three measures help separate a slow load, a slow click response and a jumping layout.

examples.title: Give images their size
examples.description: Image width and height tell the browser the picture's shape before it finishes loading.
examples.output: The browser can reserve a 3-to-2 shaped area before garden.jpg loads.

examples.title: Load lower images later
examples.description: Lazy loading delays some images until they are near the visible area.
examples.output: The browser may wait to load this lower image until the reader gets closer to it.

examples.title: Offer an image that fits
examples.description: Responsive image sources let the browser choose a suitable image size.
examples.output: With real image files at those widths, the browser chooses a source using the layout size and display density.

examples.title: Keep early scripts from blocking HTML
examples.description: A deferred classic script downloads while HTML is read and runs after parsing.
examples.output: The browser fetches club.js without stopping HTML parsing at this tag. It executes after the document is parsed.

examples.title: Load optional code when needed
examples.description: Dynamic import can load a JavaScript module when a feature is used.
examples.output: On a page with a real button and chart.js export, the chart module is requested when the feature is first opened.

examples.title: Avoid repeating layout work
examples.description: Reading layout after each style change can make the browser repeatedly calculate positions.
examples.output: The code reads all widths first, then applies the new heights.

examples.title: Schedule a visual update
examples.description: requestAnimationFrame asks the browser to run a visual update before a future paint.
examples.output: On a page with a .box element, the box moves in a scheduled visual update.

examples.title: Use a font fallback
examples.description: A fallback font shows readable words while a web font loads.
examples.output: With a real font file, text can appear in a system font first and switch when ClubText is ready.

examples.title: Understand browser caching
examples.description: A cache keeps a response so it may be reused.
examples.code:
For a versioned asset such as app.a1b2c3.js, a static host may send:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

For HTML that changes, use a policy that lets the browser check for updates.
examples.output: A file whose address changes with its contents can be cached for a long time. HTML needs a policy that still delivers updates.

examples.title: Keep a performance checklist
examples.description: A useful performance budget sets limits that matter for the page.
examples.code:
List important pages and tasks.
Track total transferred image and script sizes.
Check a slower device and network.
Review LCP, INP and CLS evidence.
Keep accessibility and readable content in every check.
Repeat after large new features.
examples.output: The project gets a repeatable check, not a one-time speed score.
